sections.on_the_job: Come here in this order: Table 1 for the allowed percentage, Table 4 for the raceway, Table 5 for insulated conductors, and Table 8 when a voltage-drop check needs resistance. One pass through a real check: three or more conductors means 40 percent from Table 1; 1/2 in EMT allows 0.122 sq in at that percentage from Table 4; the conductors on the list — two 6 AWG THHN and one 10 AWG THHN — total 0.1225 sq in from Table 5, so the run goes up to 3/4 in EMT. Do not size conduit from a memorized count you heard on another job — raceway type, insulation type, and conductor count all change the answer.
sections.plain_explanation:
Chapter 9 is not a set of wiring rules for one kind of job. It is the data the rest of the book points back to:
• Table 1 — the percentage of a raceway conductors may occupy
• Table 2 — minimum radius of conduit bends
• Table 4 — raceway inside diameters and usable areas
• Table 5 and Table 5A — insulated and compact conductor dimensions and areas
• Table 8 — conductor properties and DC resistance, the voltage-drop input
• Table 9 — AC resistance and reactance, for finer voltage-drop work
• Tables 11(A) and 11(B) — how much power a Class 2 or Class 3 source may deliver
Behind the tables sit the informative annexes — Annex B on ampacity calculation under engineering supervision, Annex C's same-size fill tables, Annex D's worked load-calculation examples, Annex I's recommended torque values. Annex material explains and illustrates; it does not add mandatory requirements on its own.
sections.title: Chapter 9 — the table room
sections.why_it_exists: Every sizing answer in the trade is only as good as the table it came from. Chapter 9 keeps the numbers in one printed place, so a fill percentage, a raceway area and a resistance all trace to the same source instead of memory and habit. The annexes sit behind a fence for a reason: a worked example shows one way through a calculation, and treating an example as a rule is how a legal installation gets failed — or an illegal one gets built.
inspection_fails: Mixed-size pull sized from an Annex C count table, which only works when every conductor is the same size and type.
Fill figured from the EMT row of Table 4 for a PVC Schedule 40 run — the raceway installed is smaller inside than the raceway calculated.
Voltage-drop check run on a resistance remembered from another conductor size instead of the Table 8 row for the conductor in hand.
Annex example cited to the inspector as if it were a Code requirement.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer treats Annex C like a requirement table: 'Annex C says nine fit, so nine are legal.' Annex C is an informative shortcut built from Tables 1, 4 and 5 for same-size conductors only. It cannot bless a mixed-size pull, and no annex overrides the tables it was built from.

sections.figure_idea: Three circles showing the same raceway with one, two, and three-plus conductors shaded to 53, 31, and 40 percent.
sections.on_the_job: Count every conductor in the run, including the equipment grounding conductor, then pick the percentage for that count before you open Tables 4 and 5. The most common house and light-commercial case is three or more conductors, so 40 percent is the column you will use most — but never use it for a one- or two-conductor pull. Short stubs earn their own number: a 1/2 in EMT nipple has a 60 percent area of 0.182 sq in in Table 4, which at 0.0133 sq in for one 12 AWG THHN is 13 conductors by fill alone.
sections.plain_explanation:
Table 1 sets the share of a raceway's inside cross-section that conductors may take up:
• 1 conductor — 53 percent
• 2 conductors — 31 percent
• 3 or more conductors — 40 percent
• A nipple 24 in or less between enclosures — 60 percent, covered on the nipple page
The percentage is taken against the raceway's total inside area in Table 4, and the conductor areas come from Table 5. Those percentages already allow for the fact that conductors do not pack like water — two round conductors side by side waste more of the circle, which is why the two-conductor number is the lowest of the three.
sections.title: Table 1 — how much of a raceway you may fill
sections.why_it_exists: A raceway filled past its percentage cannot be pulled without a fight: conductors jam at the bends, insulation skins against the raceway wall, and a damaged jacket is a fault waiting for a damp day. The limits also leave the breathing room a bundled run needs. The odd dip at two conductors is geometry, not a typo — two circles side by side waste more of the pipe than one large conductor or a bundle of three or more.
inspection_fails: Two-conductor pull figured at 40 percent instead of 31 — the raceway is overfilled on the approved calculation itself.
Equipment ground left out of the conductor count, so a three-conductor run was figured as two — wrong percentage and the ground's own area missing.
The 60 percent nipple allowance applied to a full-length run between panels.
Percentage read off one raceway's Table 4 row and applied to another — an EMT answer used for a PVC run.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is reaching for 40 percent every time because it is the familiar number. Two conductors get only 31 percent — a two-wire pull figured at 40 is overfilled before it starts. The reverse trap: 53 percent is not a bonus rate for three conductors. It belongs to a single conductor only.

sections.on_the_job: Worked check: a 1/2 in EMT nipple has a 60 percent area of 0.182 sq in in Table 4. At 0.0133 sq in for one 12 AWG THHN, that is 0.182 / 0.0133 = 13.68, so 13 conductors by fill alone. And Note 4 to Table 1 goes further than the 60%: the 310.15(C)(1) ampacity adjustment factors do NOT have to be applied to conductors in a nipple 24 in or shorter — the Code waives that check here expressly, so do not saddle the nipple with it.
sections.plain_explanation: A short raceway nipple — 24 in or less between boxes, cabinets, or similar enclosures — may be filled to 60 percent instead of the Table 1 percentages. The extra room is allowed because a short, straight stub is far easier to pull and far less likely to jam than a long run. The allowance belongs to the nipple only; the long runs on either side of it still use 53, 31, or 40 percent as their conductor count requires. Note 4 to Table 1 carries a second gift: the 310.15(C)(1) ampacity adjustment factors do not have to be applied to conductors in a nipple 24 in or shorter.
sections.title: The 60 percent nipple allowance
sections.why_it_exists: The fill percentages protect the pull and the insulation: conductors jammed into an overfilled raceway skin against the wall at every bend, and a bundled run needs room to shed heat. A nipple is short and straight, with an enclosure open at both ends, so the jam risk that drives the lower percentages barely exists — that is why the Code trades up to 60 percent there, and waives the bundling adjustment there, and only there.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is carrying the 60 percent past the nipple. The allowance ends at 24 in and at the nipple's own walls: a 30 in stub, or the full run between the same two panels, is back to 53, 31, or 40 percent. The second trap runs the other way — derating a legal nipple anyway and upsizing gear that never needed it.

sections.figure_idea: A 90-degree bend drawn with a dimension line running from the bend's center point to the conduit centerline, with two arcs shown — the tighter bender arc and the wider heat-bend arc — labelled with the two Table 2 columns.
sections.on_the_job:
A bender's shoe sets the radius for you: use the shoe made for the conduit type and size and the bend lands on the first column by construction. Heat-bent PVC is where crews get caught — form the sweep to at least the 'other bends' number, because a tight heat bend that kinks or flattens also fails the 'do not damage, do not effectively reduce the inside diameter' half of the bending sections.

Worked check: a 2 in PVC stub-up sweep formed at a 10 in centerline radius fails Table 2 by 2 in even if it looks smooth. Re-form it at 12 in or better before the concrete truck is called.
sections.plain_explanation:
Table 2 sets the smallest radius a field bend may have, measured to the centerline of the conduit — not to the inside face of the bend. It has two columns, and the bending method picks the column, not a section number:
• One-shot or full-shoe bender: the first column. The shoe is made for the conduit type and size, so a bend on the right shoe lands on this column by construction.
• All other bends: the second column. A PVC heat bend falls here, however smooth it looks.
The table is a floor, not a target. A factory sweep or a segmented bend laid out well above these numbers is fine. The printed table runs to 6 in; the sizes Sharma bends most are below.
sections.title: Table 2 — minimum radius of conduit bends
sections.why_it_exists: A bend that is too tight kinks or flattens the raceway, and a flattened bend drags on every conductor pulled through it — insulation scrapes, conductors jam, and the inside diameter the fill math assumed is no longer there. The radius floor keeps the bend gentle enough that the wire survives the pull and the conduit keeps its shape.
inspection_fails: Heat-bent PVC stub-up sweep formed at a 10 in centerline radius on 2 in conduit — Table 2 needs 12 in for other bends.
Bend kinked or flattened so the inside diameter is effectively reduced, even where the radius itself is legal.
Radius checked to the outside of the bend instead of the centerline, so a tight bend passes on paper only.
sections.exam_trap: A 2 in PVC heat bend formed at 9½ in matches Table 2, right? Wrong column. 9½ in is the one-shot / full-shoe number for 2 in; a heat bend is an 'other bend' and needs 12 in. The method picks the column before the size picks the number.

page_quiz.explain_plain: A heat bend is an 'other bend.' For 2 in, the other-bends column of Table 2 is 12 in.

sections.on_the_job: Read the row for the exact raceway you are installing, then take the column that matches your conductor count from Table 1. sections.plain_explanation:
Table 4 gives, for each raceway type and trade size, the inside diameter, the total inside area, and the usable area at each Table 1 percentage. It is the denominator of every fill check: conductor areas from Table 5 are added up, then compared against the usable area this table allows.
• Trade size is a name, not a measurement: 1/2 in EMT is actually 0.622 in inside and 0.304 sq in total, with 0.122 sq in usable at 40 percent.
• Raceway type matters as much as trade size: 1/2 in PVC Schedule 40 is a little smaller inside (0.285 sq in total, 0.114 at 40 percent), so an EMT answer does not carry over to PVC.
• PVC Schedule 80, the thick-wall PVC used where conduit is subject to physical damage, runs smaller inside than Schedule 40 at every size. Flexible metal conduit (FMC) is its own row too — close to EMT at the small sizes, but never the same row.
A fill that passes in Schedule 40 or EMT can fail in Schedule 80, so when the raceway changes, rerun the division with the new row.
sections.title: Table 4 — raceway inside dimensions and usable area
sections.why_it_exists: Every fill check is a division, and Table 4 is the bottom half of it. Use the wrong raceway's row and the answer is wrong with confidence — the crew pulls a fill that passed on paper and jams in the pipe, or an inspector reruns the math with the right row and the run fails after it is in the ground.

Trade size used as the inside diameter (1/2 in taken as a 0.500 in hole) instead of the Table 4 row.
Fill never rerun when the spec changed the raceway from Schedule 40 to Schedule 80.

sections.plain_explanation:
Table 5 gives the approximate diameter and area of insulated conductors and fixture wires, by size and insulation type. Fill is figured on the insulated conductor you are actually pulling, insulation included — not on the bare metal.
• Read three things together: the AWG size, the insulation type, and that type's column. A different insulation type in the same AWG can have a different area, so the insulation column is part of the answer.
• The table below carries the THHN / THWN / THWN-2 column — the insulation Sharma pulls most.
• Bare conductors are not sized from this table; a bare grounding conductor's area is figured from its own dimensions in Table 8.
sections.title: Table 5 — how much room an insulated conductor takes

sections.why_it_exists: Fill limits exist because a stuffed raceway damages insulation on the pull and traps heat in service. sections.title: Table 5A — compact conductor dimensions and areas
sections.plain_explanation:
Table 5A is Table 5's sibling for compact-stranded conductors. In a compact conductor the strands are compressed during manufacture, so the finished conductor is rounder and smaller across than a standard concentric-stranded conductor of the same AWG — a stranding common in larger aluminum feeder conductors.
• Fill is figured on the conductor actually in the raceway: compact conductors take their diameter and area from Table 5A, standard conductors from Table 5.
• Figuring a compact conductor from Table 5 overstates its area, so a fill can fail on paper that would pass in the raceway.
• Figuring a standard conductor from Table 5A understates it, and that direction is the violation.
The conductor's marking and its manufacturer tell you which stranding you hold.
sections.on_the_job: A 4/0 aluminum compact feeder: open Table 5A, not Table 5, before you tell the foreman the conduit size. The difference between the two tables is regularly the difference between the conduit on the truck and the next size up. Confirm the stranding before the math: "compact" is in the conductor's print legend and in the submittal. For scale, a standard-stranded 4/0 THHN reads 0.3237 sq in in Table 5 — if the reel does not say compact, the standard table is the one the fill has to carry.
sections.figure_idea: Cross-sections: concentric vs compact stranding at the same AWG, diameters compared.
sections.why_it_exists: Fill limits exist so conductors can be pulled without damage and can shed heat inside the raceway, and both protections depend on the real cross-section in the pipe. Read a compact conductor out of the standard table and you waste raceway and money on a phantom size. Read a standard conductor out of the compact table and the raceway is overfilled in fact while the paperwork says it passes — skinned insulation and a jammed pull are how that shows up.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating Table 5A as a discount table anyone can claim. It is not a smaller number for the same wire — it belongs only to conductors actually manufactured as compact strand. A standard-stranded conductor figured from Table 5A is an understated fill and a violation, however good the math looks.

sections.figure_idea: A four-step flow strip: list conductors, add Table 5 areas, pick Table 1 percent, compare in Table 4.
sections.on_the_job: Worked example, Sharma commercial: three 20 A branch circuits share one EMT — six 12 AWG THHN plus one 12 AWG THHN equipment ground. Seven conductors at 0.0133 sq in each total 0.0931 sq in. Seven conductors take the 40 percent column, and 1/2 in EMT allows 0.122 sq in at 40 percent, so it fits. If the lead picks CCA, one AWG larger under S-10, the same run is seven 10 AWG at 0.0211 — 0.1477 sq in, over 0.122 — and the raceway goes to 3/4 in EMT at 0.213. Say the steps out loud on a mixed pull before you order material. Most failed fills come from a skipped step — a ground left out of the list, an EMT row used for a PVC run, or the 40 percent column used for a two-conductor pull that only gets 31 percent.
sections.plain_explanation:
Every fill problem is the same four steps:
• Step 1 — List every conductor in the raceway, including equipment grounds, with its size and insulation type.
• Step 2 — Take each conductor's area from Table 5 (the Table 8 area for a bare conductor) and add them.
• Step 3 — Pick the Table 1 percentage from the conductor count: 53 for one conductor, 31 for two, 40 for three or more, and 60 for a nipple 24 in or less.
• Step 4 — Open Table 4 for your raceway type and take the first trade size whose usable area at that percentage is equal to or larger than your conductor total. If the total is even slightly over, go up a trade size; close does not count.
sections.sharma_note: S-01 and S-10 apply only when an example uses Sharma's sizing: commercial branch circuits are 20A minimum on 12 AWG copper, and CCA, when the lead picks it, goes one AWG size larger. sections.why_it_exists: Conductors need room. In an overfilled raceway the pull jams, insulation scrapes and stretches, and a conductor can be damaged before it ever carries a load. The percentages sit well under the raceway's full area because round conductors do not pack like water — the air between them is part of the math, and two conductors side by side waste the most space, which is why two get the lowest share, 31 percent. Four steps, done in order, make the answer come from the tables instead of from how the pull feels.

sections.exam_trap: The trap is the two-conductor percentage. Three or more conductors get 40 percent, so 40 feels like the default — but two conductors get only 31 percent, the lowest number in Table 1. The second trap on this page: leaving the equipment ground off the list because 'it carries no current.' Fill does not care what a conductor carries. If it is in the raceway, its area is in the total.

sections.on_the_job: Default to rounding down. Use the 0.8 round-up only when every conductor in the raceway is truly the same size and type, and be ready to show the inspector the division. Mixed sizes never get the round-up — add their areas instead.
sections.plain_explanation:
When every conductor is the same size and type, the count is one division: the raceway's usable area divided by one conductor's area.
• Worked example: how many 12 AWG THHN fit in 1/2 in EMT? The 40 percent area is 0.122 sq in and one 12 AWG THHN is 0.0133 sq in, so 0.122 / 0.0133 = 9.17 — the answer is 9, because a tenth of a conductor does not exist.
• One exception, from the Chapter 9 notes: when all conductors are the same size and the division leaves a decimal of 0.8 or more, the count may be rounded up to the next whole conductor — 8 AWG THHN in 3/4 in EMT is 0.213 / 0.0366 = 5.82, so 6 are permitted by that note.
sections.title: Same-size fill — divide, then round down
sections.why_it_exists: The round-down rule is the raceway's safety margin doing its quiet work: 9.17 is a paper number, and the 0.17 that 'almost fits' is exactly the conductor that would have been skinned on the pull or cooked in the bundle. The 0.8 exception is narrow on purpose — it trusts the geometry only when every conductor is identical, so the packing the table assumed is the packing you actually get.
sections.exam_trap: Two traps share this page. First: rounding 9.17 up to 10 because 'it is close' — the round-up exists only at a decimal of 0.8 or more. Second: using the 0.8 round-up on a mixed-size pull. Mixed sizes never divide and never round up; their areas are added, conductor by conductor.

sections.on_the_job: Write each conductor's area on the takeoff, not just the sum. When a run fails by a hair — like the 0.1225 example, over by five ten-thousandths — the written list is how you prove the next trade size was required and not a guess. It is also how the next electrician, adding a circuit to that raceway next year, knows exactly how much room is left: in the 3/4 in EMT from example one, 0.213 - 0.1225 = 0.0905 sq in of the 40 percent allowance is still open.
sections.plain_explanation:
Mixed sizes cannot be divided; each conductor contributes its own Table 5 area and the total is compared with the Table 4 area for the raceway, at the Table 1 percentage for the count.
• Worked example one: two 6 AWG THHN plus one 10 AWG THHN total 2 x 0.0507 + 0.0211 = 0.1225 sq in — just over the 0.122 sq in that 1/2 in EMT allows at 40 percent, so the run goes to 3/4 in EMT at 0.213.
• Worked example two: three 1/0 THHN plus a 6 AWG THHN ground total 3 x 0.1855 + 0.0507 = 0.6072 sq in; 1-1/4 in EMT allows 0.598 and is too small, so 1-1/2 in EMT at 0.814 is the answer.
There is no rounding a mixed total down to fit. Over is over, even by 0.0005 sq in.
sections.title: Mixed-size fill — add the areas
sections.why_it_exists: A mixed pull is where the same-size shortcuts break. One large conductor eats area that a division method assumes is shared evenly, and a total that lands a hair over the limit does not pull like one that lands a hair under — it jams at the bend and skins insulation. Adding the areas one conductor at a time is slower, and it is the only arithmetic that matches what is physically in the pipe.
inspection_fails: Mixed-size pull figured by dividing the raceway area by the largest conductor's area — the smaller conductors' real areas never entered the calculation.
Conductor total rounded down to the raceway allowance on the fill schedule — 0.1225 shown as 0.122.
Ground left off the mixed list; the total passes without it and fails with it.
Annex C count used for a mixed-size pull.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer rounds: '0.1225 is basically 0.122 — it fits.' Fill has no 'basically.' The only round-up in Chapter 9 belongs to same-size division that leaves a remainder of 0.8 or more, and it never applies to a mixed-size total. 0.1225 sq in of conductor in a 0.122 sq in allowance is an overfilled raceway.

sections.figure_idea: A conductor list with the ground line highlighted, showing an insulated ground routed to Table 5 and a bare ground routed to Table 8.
sections.on_the_job: On every fill list, write the ground as its own line with its own area before you add. A Florida home run in 1/2 in EMT: three 12 AWG THHN circuit conductors at 0.0133 sq in each total 0.0399 sq in. With an insulated 12 AWG THHN ground the list totals 0.0532 sq in; with a bare 12 AWG ground it totals 0.0450 sq in. Both fit the 0.122 sq in that 1/2 in EMT allows at 40 percent — but on a tight pull the ground's line is the difference between passing and going up a trade size. Say on the list whether the ground is bare or insulated, and take its area from the right table.
sections.plain_explanation:
An equipment grounding conductor takes up room in the raceway like any other conductor, so it counts in fill — a note to Table 1 says so directly, and says to use the conductor's actual dimensions.
• Insulated ground: take its area from Table 5, in the column for its insulation type. A 12 AWG THHN ground is 0.0133 sq in, the same as any 12 AWG THHN.
• Bare ground: there is no insulation to measure, so Table 5 has no row for it. Take its diameter from Table 8 and use the area of that circle — a bare 12 AWG is 0.081 in across, about 0.0051 sq in.
• One ground, counted once: a shared equipment ground serving several circuits in one raceway still gets its one line on the list.
Leaving the ground out is the most common reason a fill calculation passes on paper and jams in the field.
sections.section: Tables 5 and 8, grounds and bare conductors
sections.title: Grounds count, and bare conductors use Table 8
sections.why_it_exists: Fill is physical, not electrical. The ground carries no load current, but the pull does not care — every conductor in the pipe adds friction on the bends and one more chance to skin insulation. A calculation that leaves the ground out approves a raceway the wire cannot actually get through, and the crew finds out halfway through the pull, with the insulation paying for it.
inspection_fails: Fill calculation on the permit set omits the equipment grounding conductor — the raceway is over its Table 1 percentage once the ground is counted.
Bare ground figured at the insulated Table 5 area, or an insulated ground figured as bare — wrong table for the conductor as installed.
Pull jammed mid-run and insulation damaged on a raceway that only passed because the ground was left off the list.
Fill schedule shows no ground line at all for a raceway that contains one.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: 'The ground does not count — it carries no current.' That mixes up two different checks. Current-carrying status matters for the ampacity adjustment in 310.15(C)(1); fill is about space, and the ground takes space. Count it, at its real area: Table 5 if it is insulated, Table 8 if it is bare.

sections.florida_note: Annex B is informative. The mandatory ampacity rules are the Chapter 3 articles as adopted in Florida; an annex calculation supports an engineered design, it does not replace the adopted tables on its own.
sections.on_the_job: The plans for a small commercial job show a feeder sized smaller than Table 310.16 gives for the load, noted 'ampacity per Annex B — engineering supervision.' Nobody on the crew re-runs that math, and nobody talks it away either. Sharma crews size conductors from Table 310.16 and the Chapter 3 pages, full stop. If a plan shows an ampacity that only works 'per Annex B' or 'per engineering supervision,' that is a Mike-and-the-engineer item: do not match it with a field guess, and do not downsize a conductor on an annex number nobody calculated for this job.
sections.plain_explanation:
Informative Annex B is the Code's application information for calculating conductor ampacity under engineering supervision — the formula route that accounts for load diversity, conductor arrangement, duct banks and ambient conditions instead of reading a single table cell. Its own tables give ampacities for specific free-air and underground electrical duct arrangements that Table 310.16 does not cover. Two limits define it:
• It is informative, not mandatory. No annex number is a requirement an inspector can cite the way a Chapter 3 section can be cited.
• It is engineering work. The calculation has to be performed and documented for the actual installation by a qualified person — never estimated in the field.
Field sizing stays on the adopted tables: Table 310.16, with the correction and adjustment factors of 310.15. An Annex B number belongs to the design that produced it, with that design's duct spacing, soil conditions and loading assumptions attached.

sections.why_it_exists: Table 310.16 is built on standard assumptions about conductor count, ambient and arrangement. A real duct bank or an unusual grouping does not always match those assumptions, and one table cell cannot know your soil or your spacing. The formula route exists so an engineer can model the installation that is actually being built. The supervision requirement is the guardrail: an ampacity nobody calculated is just a smaller conductor with a story attached, and an undersized conductor runs hot for the life of the building.
inspection_fails: Feeder installed one size under Table 310.16 with 'per Annex B' written on the takeoff and no engineering calculation on file.
Duct bank built with different conduit spacing than the engineered design the ampacity was figured from — the calculation no longer matches the installation.
Annex B ampacity claimed at inspection with no documentation of who calculated it, or for what conditions.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: 'Annex B permits a smaller conductor than Table 310.16 whenever the load calculation shows diversity.' Wrong twice. Annex B is informative, so by itself it permits nothing, and its numbers come from an engineering calculation performed and documented for the actual installation — not from a diversity note in a load calc, and never from a field estimate. Without the documented calculation behind it, the table size stands.

sections.figure_idea: Two paths to the same answer side by side: the long division 0.122 / 0.0133 = 9 and a blank annex lookup card also landing on 9, with a red line through a mixed-size pull trying to use the shortcut.
sections.florida_note: Annex C is informative, not mandatory. The mandatory fill limits are in Chapter 9 Tables 1, 4, and 5 as adopted; the annex is a convenience for one narrow case.
sections.on_the_job: Use Annex C to sanity-check a same-size count in seconds, then be able to show the Tables 4 and 5 division behind it: 0.122 sq in of usable area in 1/2 in EMT, divided by 0.0133 sq in for one 12 AWG THHN, is 9.17 — so 9, the same 9 the annex prints. If the annex count and your division disagree, trust neither until you find which input — raceway type, insulation type, or ground — was different.
sections.plain_explanation:
Annex C is a set of pre-worked fill tables for the narrow case where every conductor in the raceway is the same size and type: you look up the raceway and read off a maximum count instead of dividing. It is the Tables 1, 4, and 5 math done ahead of time, and it agrees with that math — the v1 example of nine 12 AWG THHN in 1/2 in EMT matches the Annex C table for that combination.
• What it answers: one raceway, one conductor size, one insulation type — a maximum count.
• What it cannot answer: a mixed-size pull, a different insulation type than the table assumes, or a bare ground.
This book does not reproduce its tables; learn the division and use the annex only as a check.
sections.title: Annex C — the same-size shortcut, and its limits
sections.why_it_exists: Annex C is a shortcut, and shortcuts get stretched. Used outside its one narrow case, it hands you a confident number with the wrong inputs baked in — a mixed pull 'checked' against a same-size table is overfilled before the first conductor moves. The fill percentages protect the pull and the insulation; the division is how you know they hold. The annex is only a second pair of eyes on that math.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is using Annex C because it is fast, on a pull it was never built for. The annex assumes every conductor is the same size and type. The moment the pull mixes sizes, changes insulation type, or adds a bare ground, there is no annex row for it — and a count read off the wrong table is just a wrong count with a citation.

sections.figure_idea: The 12 AWG stranded copper row highlighted at 1.98 ohm/kft, with a downhill staircase showing resistance falling as AWG steps up to 6.
sections.on_the_job: A Sharma example, worked from this table: a 20 A load at the end of a 75 ft one-way run on 12 AWG copper. VD = 2 × L × R × I ÷ 1000 = 2 × 75 × 1.98 × 20 ÷ 1000 = 5.94 V — about 5 percent of 120 V, past the 3 percent recommendation. On 10 AWG (1.24 Ω/kft) the same run drops 3.72 V — still past it. On 8 AWG (0.778 Ω/kft) it drops 2.33 V, about 2 percent — inside. Three things make the check honest: the right metal column, the right stranding row, and resistance per thousand feet — the formula divides by 1000 because the table is priced per thousand feet, not per foot.
sections.plain_explanation:
Table 8 describes the conductor itself: area in circular mils, stranding, overall diameter, and direct-current resistance at 75 °C in ohms per thousand feet, for copper and for aluminum.
• Read the metal column first — copper and aluminum are different sets of numbers on the same page.
• Read the stranding row that matches the conductor in hand. Solid and stranded versions of the same AWG have slightly different resistance.
• Resistance falls hard as size rises: stranded copper runs 3.14 Ω/kft at 14 AWG and 0.491 Ω/kft at 6 AWG. That drop is exactly why upsizing cures voltage drop.
The table below carries the full run of common stranded-copper sizes, so a voltage-drop check never has to stop at 6 AWG.
sections.title: Table 8 — conductor properties and DC resistance

tables.caption: Table 8 — stranded uncoated copper, DC resistance at 75 °C

sections.why_it_exists: Resistance is what turns a long run into a voltage-drop problem: every ohm in the loop drops voltage the load never sees. Table 8 is the honest source for that resistance — by metal, by stranding, at a stated temperature. Guess the resistance, or read the wrong row, and the calculation is fiction with good formatting.
inspection_fails: Voltage-drop calculation run on the solid-conductor row for stranded conductors — resistance understated, drop understated.
Drop figured from the copper column for an aluminum feeder.
Calculation worked in ohms per foot against a per-thousand-feet table — the reported drop is off by a factor of 1000.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: reading the solid row for a stranded conductor — or the copper column for an aluminum run — because the AWG matches. Table 8's answer depends on metal and stranding, not just size. The other classic: forgetting the ÷ 1000 and reporting a drop a thousand times too big.

sections.on_the_job: If a CCA run needs a voltage-drop answer, do not borrow the aluminum column and report the result as the CCA drop — the aluminum number belongs to aluminum. Get the maker's DC resistance for the actual cable at 75 degrees C, write the source on the calculation, and only then run the formula. If that number is not on hand, the honest status is 'not yet calculated,' and that is what goes on the takeoff.
sections.plain_explanation:
Copper-clad aluminum is not in Table 8. The printed table carries copper — uncoated and coated — and aluminum, and nothing else: no CCA column, no CCA row, and this book does not invent one.
• Ampacity is a different question. There, Table 310.16 reads CCA in its aluminum and copper-clad aluminum column, and S-10 sizes CCA one AWG larger.
• Voltage drop is where the gap bites, because the resistance has to describe the actual conductor. The aluminum column describes aluminum, and it is not a CCA value: a drop computed from it must never be reported as a CCA conductor's drop.
• A CCA resistance has to come from the cable maker's data for the actual product, at the operating temperature. Until a cited manufacturer value for the CCA product Sharma installs is on file, this book publishes no CCA voltage-drop figure — the same open point carried on C3-310.16-CCA.

sections.on_the_job: Use the real load current, not the breaker size, unless the load truly is the breaker size. sections.plain_explanation:
Voltage drop is the voltage used up pushing current through the conductor's resistance, out and back. For a single-phase circuit the approximation used here is:
VD = 2 x L x R x I / 1000
• 2 — the round trip. Current travels the length twice, out on one conductor and back on the other. It is the most-forgotten factor in the whole calculation.
• L — the one-way length in feet, as the run is actually routed.
• R — the conductor's resistance from Table 8, in ohms per thousand feet. Stranded copper: 12 AWG is 1.98, 10 AWG is 1.24, 8 AWG is 0.778.
• I — the actual load current in amps, not the breaker size.
• / 1000 — Table 8 is priced per thousand feet, so the division puts the answer in volts.
Finish by turning volts into a percentage: VD divided by the system voltage, times 100. Percent is what the 3 percent and 5 percent recommendations are measured against.
sections.sharma_note: S-01 example sizing only: on a commercial job the starting conductor is 12 AWG copper minimum because Sharma requires 20A branch circuits — if the voltage-drop check then fails, upsize from there. The Code does not impose Sharma's 20A minimum.
sections.title: Voltage drop — the single-phase method
sections.why_it_exists: Voltage lost in the wire is voltage the load never sees. Motors start hard and run hot on low voltage, lights dim, electronics complain — and the lost energy heats the conductor run instead of doing work at the load. The drop grows with length, current and resistance, which is why a circuit that is fine at 30 ft can be a problem at 130 ft on the same breaker.

Drop figured at the breaker rating for a load drawing half that, with the wire upsized two sizes past what the load needs.
sections.exam_trap: The classic trap drops the 2: VD = L x R x I / 1000. That figures only the trip out and reports half the real drop — a run that truly drops 6.34V 'passes' at 3.17V on paper. If a voltage-drop answer looks too good for a long run, check for the missing round trip first.

sections.why_it_exists: Every foot of conductor is a small resistance in series with the load, and the current crosses it twice — out and back. Drop grows with length and with current, so a run that serves a load fine at 20 ft can starve the same load at 100 ft. The missing volts never reach the load: lights run dim, and a motor draws more current to make the same power and runs hotter doing it. Working the formula one size at a time is how you land on the smallest conductor that actually serves the load — no guessing, no wasted copper.

For a balanced three-phase circuit, the round-trip factor of 2 is replaced by 1.732, the square root of 3: VD = 1.732 x L x R x I / 1000.
• L is still the one-way length in feet.
• R is still the Table 8 resistance, in ohms per thousand feet.
• I is the load current.
Stated plainly, this is an approximation — it borrows DC resistance from Table 8 for an AC system, and larger conductors, steel raceways, and power factor can move the real answer, which is the work Table 9 exists for. • Feeder plus the branch circuit it supplies: about 5 percent total.

sections.on_the_job:
If a voltage-drop answer matters enough to fight over — a long feeder, a big motor, a plan review comment — do not settle it with the Table 8 approximation. Flag it for Mike to run with Table 9 and the actual raceway and power factor.

Worked example with the effective-Z column: a 208 V three-phase feeder carrying 100 A at 0.85 power factor, 200 ft one-way, on 2 AWG copper in PVC (Z = 0.19 ohm/kft). VD = 1.732 × 200 × 0.19 × 100 / 1000 = 6.58 V, about 3.2 percent of 208 V — over the 3 percent recommendation on the feeder alone, so the design conversation starts at 1 AWG or 1/0, not at hope.
sections.plain_explanation:
Table 9 is the next step past Table 8 for voltage drop. Its full title is 'Alternating-Current Resistance and Reactance for 600-Volt Cables, 3-Phase, 60 Hz, 75 °C — Three Single Conductors in Conduit,' and instead of DC resistance alone it gives, in ohms to neutral per 1000 ft:
• Inductive reactance for all wires — one value for PVC or aluminum conduit, and a higher one for steel.
• Alternating-current resistance for uncoated copper and for aluminum.
• Effective impedance Z at 0.85 power factor — the number that already blends resistance and reactance for the drop formula.
A magnetic steel raceway raises reactance and, in the larger sizes, AC resistance as well. The AC resistance column tracks Table 8 closely at small sizes and climbs above it in steel conduit as sizes grow.
The table's Note 1 limits its values to conductors at 75 °C under the conditions its title states. This page's teaching is when to reach for it — large conductors, long three-phase runs, steel raceway, or a Table 8 approximation that lands near a limit — and to run those cases from the printed table rather than from memory. Common copper sizes are carried in the tables below; aluminum and sizes above 4/0 stay in the printed table.
The 3 percent / 5 percent voltage-drop figures are Informational Note recommendations, not requirements.

Table 9 exists so that argument is settled with the real impedance.

sections.title: Tables 11(A) and 11(B) — how much power a Class 2 or Class 3 source may deliver
sections.plain_explanation:
Tables 11(A) and 11(B) are the numbers behind the words 'power limited.' For Class 2 and Class 3 circuits, the tables cap what the power source may deliver — maximum circuit voltage, maximum current, and maximum volt-amperes — with one table for ac sources and one for dc sources. Each table splits sources two ways: inherently limited sources, whose construction keeps them inside the limits under any load or fault, and sources that are not inherently limited and therefore rely on overcurrent protection sized from the table. Article 725 sends you here to decide whether a transformer or supply really is a Class 2 source; a 'Class 2' claim on a nameplate is checked against these tables, not taken on faith.
• The nameplate ceiling both classes live under: 100 VA maximum.
• A Class 2 source running over 30 V is held to 0.005 A — five milliamps — which is why Class 2 earns its shock-safe reputation.
• At 20 V a Class 2 nameplate may show up to 5.0 A; the current ceiling falls as the voltage rises.
sections.on_the_job: A door-control transformer marked Class 2: the table row for its voltage is what makes that marking true, and it is also what earns the wiring-method freedoms Chapter 7 gives Class 2 circuits. No table match, no Class 2 treatment — the circuit is wired like power. Read the nameplate VA before you land the conductors: at 100 VA or less the supply can be a Class 2 source; a 250 VA transformer cannot, whatever is printed on the cable jacket.

sections.why_it_exists: Class 2 wiring gets freedoms no power circuit gets — lighter wiring methods and relaxed separation — because the source cannot deliver enough energy to start a fire or give a dangerous shock. That bargain only holds if the source truly stays inside the table. A supply that can push past its row is a power circuit wearing a Class 2 label, wired with Class 2 freedoms it never earned.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is believing the words on the jacket. 'Class 2' is a conclusion the tables reach about a source, not a description of the cable or the transformer frame. The exam version: a source that is not inherently limited is still not a Class 2 source until it is paired with overcurrent protection sized from the table — the protection is part of the source.

sections.figure_idea: A flowchart from a house's load list through demand factors to a service size, with a signpost pointing back to Chapter 2 and 220.82.
sections.florida_note: Annex D is informative. The mandatory calculation rules are the Chapter 2 articles as adopted in Florida; the annex only illustrates them.
sections.on_the_job: Work a Sharma example fresh from the actual house, in the annex's order. General loads first, on the optional method of 220.82(B): a 2,000 sq ft house takes 2,000 × 3 VA = 6,000 VA for floor area, plus two small-appliance circuits at 1,500 VA each and the laundry circuit at 1,500 VA — 10,500 VA before demand. The first 10 kVA counts at 100 percent and the remaining 500 VA at 40 percent, so the general-load demand is 10,200 VA; heating and cooling are then selected separately under 220.82(C), largest selection only. Keep the arithmetic with the estimate so Mike can re-run it. If your total and the annex pattern disagree, the inputs are wrong somewhere, not the pattern.
sections.plain_explanation:
Annex D shows the load-calculation articles worked end to end on example buildings: add the loads the articles name, apply the demand factors the articles allow, and arrive at a service or feeder size. The 2020 annex works eight example families:
• D1 — a one-family dwelling by the standard method, with and without air conditioning.
• D2 — a one-family dwelling by the optional method of 220.82, including a heat-pump version with backup heat.
• D3 — a store building.
• D4 and D5 — multifamily dwellings; D5 is served at 208Y/120 volts, three-phase.
• D6 — maximum demand for range loads from Table 220.55.
• D7 — dwelling service conductors sized with 310.12.
• D8 — motor conductors and protection under Article 430.
This book teaches that method and points you to the real work in Chapter 2 — especially the optional dwelling calculation of 220.82 — rather than copying an annex example. A Sharma example must be computed fresh from the actual house, labeled as a Sharma example, and checked; an annex example is a pattern to follow, not a number to borrow for a different building.
sections.title: Annex D — worked load-calculation examples
sections.why_it_exists: Services are sized from calculations, not from what the last house took. The worked examples exist so the method stays visible: every load the articles name, in the articles' order, with only the demand factors the articles allow. Skip a named load or invent a demand factor and the service is the wrong size with confident-looking paperwork behind it.
inspection_fails: Service size on the permit set copied from an annex example instead of calculated from the building's actual loads.
Load calculation missing a load the articles name — no laundry circuit, or a fastened-in-place appliance left off the list.
Demand factor applied to a load that the article does not allow it for.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: lifting a finished number out of an annex example because the house “looks about the same.” The examples are patterns, not answers — D1's total belongs to D1's house. A Sharma service size is computed from the actual loads of the actual building and labeled as a Sharma example.

sections.figure_idea: A lug with a torque wrench, and a decision ladder beside it: equipment marking, manufacturer instruction, then recommended table.
sections.on_the_job: On a Sharma service change in Orlando, work the ladder in order. Read the panel and lug markings first — the value printed there is the rule. No marking on the equipment? Go to the manufacturer instructions for the gear. Only when neither exists do the Annex I tables in the printed book supply the number. Whatever the source, the tightening is done with a torque tool, not by feel, on service and feeder lugs — and the source of the value goes in the job notes so the next person can check it.
sections.plain_explanation:
Informative Annex I is titled “Recommended Tightening Torque Tables from UL Standard 486A-B.” It collects recommended tightening-torque values for connections in three tables:
• Table I.1 — screws No. 10 and larger, including split-bolt and other connectors.
• Table I.2 — slotted head screws smaller than No. 10, intended for use with conductors 8 AWG and smaller.
• Table I.3 — screws with recessed Allen or square drives.
The annex is a fallback, not the first stop. 110.14(D) makes the manufacturer's stated torque the rule, achieved by an approved means such as a torque tool. The annex tables serve only the connection where the equipment gives no torque value and none can be obtained from the manufacturer. This page publishes no torque values — torque comes off the equipment marking, the manufacturer's instructions, or the annex tables in the printed book, never from memory.
sections.title: Annex I — recommended tightening torque
sections.why_it_exists: A loose lug is a heater. A connection that is not tightened to its specified torque works loose under load cycling, overheats, and can arc or burn — failed services start here. An over-tightened lug is no better: it deforms the conductor and the connector. The specified value exists so the connection is clamped the way it was tested and listed.
inspection_fails: Feeder lug found loose with heat-discolored insulation — the connection was tightened by feel, no torque tool used (110.14(D)).
Torque taken from a general recommended table where the equipment label stated its own value — the label governs (110.14(D)).
Split-bolt tap connection made up with no manufacturer torque value obtained and no torque record — redo with a torque tool and document the value.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: reaching for the Annex I table first because it is printed in the back of the book. The annex is the last resort. Where the equipment marking or the manufacturer states a torque, 110.14(D) makes that value the requirement, and a general recommended table does not override it.

sections.on_the_job:
When someone quotes an annex at you on a job, ask the deciding question: is that in a mandatory section, or in an annex or a note? Both can be good practice; only one can be enforced as written, and knowing which keeps you from arguing the wrong point with an inspector.

Example: a Marion County inspector walks a rough-in with Annex C open on his phone. The shortcut is a fine check, but a correction has to cite Table 1 and Table 4 — the annex cannot carry it.
sections.plain_explanation:
The annexes sit behind the mandatory chapters as explanation, examples, and reference data. An annex is informative only: unless an adopting ordinance specifically adopts it, its content is not a requirement an inspector can cite the way a numbered article section can be cited. That is the same status the 3 percent and 5 percent voltage-drop figures carry as Informational Notes.
• What an annex can do: explain a rule, work an example, or carry reference data a crew can use.
• What it cannot do: add a requirement, or take one away.
This chapter covers the annexes Sharma work actually touches: C for same-size fill checks, D for calculation examples, and I for torque. Annex B has its own page (C9-ANNEXB), scoped the same way — what it is, when it is used, and no reproduced ampacity tables. Table 5A and Tables 11(A)/(B) now have their own pages too.
Still held back: Table 10 (stranding), Table 12 (PLFA power source limits), and the annex letters not listed as covered — not confirmed against the printed 2020 book, and this book does not invent an annex.
The 2020 informative annexes run A through J: A product safety standards, B ampacity calculation, C same-size fill tables, D examples, E types of construction, F critical operations power systems, G SCADA, H administration and enforcement, I torque tables from UL 486A-B, and J ADA standards. There is no Annex K in the 2020 book.

sections.why_it_exists: Crews and inspectors talk past each other when nobody says which kind of text they are quoting. The informative label settles the argument before it starts: an annex can teach and persuade, but a correction notice has to trace to a mandatory section. It cuts the other way too: a good annex practice — Annex D's examples, Annex I's torque values — is worth following even though nobody can cite you for skipping it.
inspection_fails: A correction argued down by quoting Annex D back at the inspector, instead of answering the mandatory section the correction actually cites.
Annex I torque values skipped because 'the annex is not mandatory' — then loose lugs overheat. Informative does not mean useless.
A bid priced off an annex example treated as a code minimum, adding work the mandatory sections never required.
sections.exam_trap: Annex D works an example one way, so that way is required? No. The examples show one compliant path through the mandatory sections; the requirement lives in the sections, not in the example. Annex C's fill tables are the same: they shortcut Table 1 and Table 4, they do not replace them.
